No handwritten homework reports are accepted for this course. We work with Git and GitHub. Efficient and abundant use of Git, e.g., frequent and well-documented commits, is an important criterion for grading your homework.

  1. Apply for the Student Developer Pack at GitHub using your UCLA email. You’ll get GitHub Pro account for free (unlimited public and private repositories).

  2. Create a private repository biostat-203b-2026-winter and add Hua-Zhou and TA team (BowenZhang2001 for Lec 1; Tomoki-Okuno and yucais for Lec 82) as your collaborators with write permission.

  3. Top directories of the repository should be hw1, hw2, … Maintain two branches main and develop. The develop branch will be your main playground, the place where you develop solution (code) to homework problems and write up report. The main branch will be your presentation area. Submit your homework files (Quarto file qmd, html file converted by Quarto, all code and extra data sets to reproduce results) in the main branch.

  4. After each homework due date, course reader and instructor will check out your main branch for grading. Tag each of your homework submissions with tag names hw1, hw2, … Tagging time will be used as your submission time. That means if you tag your hw1 submission after deadline, penalty points will be deducted for late submission.

  5. After this course, you can make this repository public and use it to demonstrate your skill sets on job market.

These data files are distributed as .csv.gz files instead of .csv (comma separated values) files because MIMIC-IV data files are large, and compressing them with gzip (.gz) significantly reduces their file size, making them easier to store and transfer. The .csv.gz format allows users to access the data without needing to decompress the entire file, which is more efficient for handling big data. Compressed files are faster to download and transfer, which is important for large datasets distributed over the internet. Modern data analysis tools such as R, Python, and SQL can read .csv.gz files directly without manual decompression, enabling scalable and reproducivle workflows. Leaving files compressed prevents the creation of multiple large uncompressed copies, which aligns with best practices for large clinical datasets. Accodring to the MIMIC-IV website, the hosp folder contains hospital-level data such as admissions, diagnoses, procedures, and laboratory results. The icu folder contains ICU-specific data such as ICU stays, vital signs, and bedside measurements. Storing these large tables in compressed form is essential for efficient storage and analysis.

  1. Briefly describe what Bash commands zcat, zless, zmore, and zgrep do.

zcat is a command that allows you to view the contents of a compressed .gz file without decompressing it. It outputs the uncompressed data to the standard output, which can be piped to other commands for further processing. It prints the uncompressed contents of a .gz file directly to the terminal (or pipes) without permanently decompressing the file. It is commonly used to stream compressed data into other commands like wc, awk, or head.

zless is a command that allows you to view the contents of a compressed .gz file interactively, similar to the less command for uncompressed files. It provides an interactive interface for navigating through the contents of the compressed file, allowing you to scroll up and down, search for specific text, and exit when finished. It is useful for quickly browsing large compressed files without needing to decompress them first.

zmore allows you to view a compressed .gz file one page/screen at a time, similar to the more command for uncompressed files. It is a simpler pager than zless, providing basic functionality for scrolling through the contents of the compressed file. It is less feature-rich than zless but can be used for quick viewing of compressed files when you don’t need the advanced navigation features of zless. It is less flexible than zless but useful for quick viewing of compressed files when you don’t need the advanced navigation features of zless.

zgrep (g — global (search the whole file), re — regular expression (pattern), p — print matching lines) allows you to search for specific patterns or text within a compressed .gz file, similar to the more command for uncompressed files. You can use zgrep to search for specific keywords, phrases, or regular expressions within the contents of a .gz file without needing to decompress it first. It is useful for quickly finding relevant information in large compressed files without the overhead of decompression.

  1. (Looping in Bash) What’s the output of the following bash script?
for datafile in ~/mimic/hosp/{a,l,pa}*.gz
do
  ls -l $datafile
done

The output of the bash script will be a list of the files in the ~/mimic/hosp/ directory that match the pattern {a,l,pa}*.gz. This pattern means that it will look for files that start with ‘a’, ‘l’, or ‘pa’ and end with ‘.gz’. The ls -l command will display the details of each matching file, including permissions, number of links, owner, group, size, and timestamp. The output will show the file names along with their respective details for all files in the hosp directory that match the specified pattern.

Each hadm_id identifies a hospitalization. How many hospitalizations are in this data file?

How many unique patients (identified by subject_id) are in this data file? Do they match the number of patients listed in the patients.csv.gz file? (Hint: combine Linux commands zcat <, head/tail, awk, sort, uniq, wc, and so on.)

# Stream the compressed admissions file without decompressing it.
# Remove the header line to avoid counting column names as data.
# Extract the subject_id column (first column) using awk.
# Sort and remove duplicates, then count unique patients.

zcat < ~/mimic/hosp/admissions.csv.gz \
| tail -n +2 \
| awk -F',' '{print $1}' \
| sort \
| uniq \
| wc -l
  223452
# Stream the compressed patients file.
# Skip the header row.
# Count the total number of rows, which corresponds to total patients.

zcat < ~/mimic/hosp/patients.csv.gz \
| tail -n +2 \
| wc -l
  364627

The number of unique patients identified by subject_id in admissions.csv.gz is 223,452, whereas the patients.csv.gz file contains 364,627 patients. These values do not match because the patients table includes all patients in the dataset, while the admissions table contains only those who had hospital admissions.

Discuss the trade off between storage and speed for big data files. (Hint: gzip -dk < FILENAME.gz > ./FILENAME. Remember to delete the large labevents.csv file after the exercise.)

rm labevents.csv

The compressed file labevents.csv.gz is significantly smaller (occupies significantly less disk space) than the uncompressed file labevents.csv, demonstrating the storage efficiency of gzip compression. However, when it comes to speed, the uncompressed version is much faster to process with wc -l compared to the compressed version using zcat. This is because decompressing the file on-the-fly with zcat adds overhead, especially for large files. The trade-off between storage and speed for big data files is that while compression saves disk space and can reduce transfer times, it can also slow down data processing due to the need for decompression. For large datasets, it may be more efficient to keep files compressed and use tools that can read compressed files directly, rather than decompressing them first.Streaming compressed files with zcat reduces storage requirements and is often preferred for large datasets, while working with uncompressed files can improve processing speed at the cost of increased disk usage. This illustrates the trade-off between storage efficiency and computational performance when working with big data.

Q4. Who’s popular in Pride and Prejudice

  1. You and your friend just have finished reading Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen. Among the four main characters in the book, Elizabeth, Jane, Lydia, and Darcy, your friend thinks that Darcy was the most mentioned. You, however, are certain it was Elizabeth. Obtain the full text of the novel from http://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/42671/pg42671.txt and save to your local folder.
wget -nc http://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/42671/pg42671.txt

Explain what wget -nc does. Do not put this text file pg42671.txt in Git.

The command wget is a utility for downloading files from the web. The -nc option stands for “no clobber,” which means that if the file already exists in the current directory, wget will not download it again and will skip the download. This prevents overwriting an existing file with the same name, which is useful to avoid unnecessary downloads and to preserve any existing data. In this case, if pg42671.txt already exists in the local folder, running wget -nc will simply skip the download and keep the existing file intact.

Complete the following loop to tabulate the number of times each of the four characters is mentioned using Linux commands.

wget -nc http://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/42671/pg42671.txt
for char in Elizabeth Jane Lydia Darcy
do
  echo $char:
  grep -i "$char" pg42671.txt | wc -l
done

Results: Elizabeth: 633 Jane: 289 Lydia: 167 Darcy: 415

  1. What’s the difference between the following two commands?
echo 'hello, world' > test1.txt

and

echo 'hello, world' >> test2.txt

The > operator redirects output to a file and overwrites the file if it already exists, replacing any previous content. In contrast, the >> operator redirects output by appending it to the end of a file, preserving the existing contents.

  1. Using your favorite text editor (e.g., vi), type the following and save the file as middle.sh:
#!/bin/sh
# Select lines from the middle of a file.
# Usage: bash middle.sh filename end_line num_lines
head -n "$2" "$1" | tail -n "$3"

Using chmod to make the file executable by the owner, and run

./middle.sh pg42671.txt 20 5

Explain the output. Explain the meaning of "$1", "$2", and "$3" in this shell script. Why do we need the first line of the shell script?

The output of the command ./middle.sh pg42671.txt 20 5 will display lines 16 to 20 of the file pg42671.txt. The script uses head to select the first 20 lines of the file and then tail to select the last 5 lines from that selection, effectively giving us lines 16-20. In the shell script, “$1”, “$2”, and “$3” are positional parameters that represent the arguments passed to the script when it is executed. “$1” refers to the first argument (filename), “$2” refers to the second argument (end_line), and “$3” refers to the third argument (num_lines). These parameters allow the script to be flexible and reusable with different inputs. The first line of the shell script, #!/bin/sh, is called a shebang. It specifies the interpreter that should be used to execute the script. In this case, it indicates that the script should be run using the Bourne shell (sh). This line is important because it ensures that the script is executed with the correct shell, which can affect how the commands within the script are interpreted and executed.

history | tail

Interpretation: The history command displays a list of previously executed commands in the current shell session. By piping it to tail, we can see only the last few entries, which gives us a quick overview of the most recent commands that were run in the terminal. When executed inside a Quarto Bash chunk, the history may be empty because the chunk runs in a new non-interactive shell session.

Q7. AI assistant

Which AI assistants (e.g., GitHub Copilot) do you use when working on this assignment? Which AI model (e.g., GPT-5 mini, GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5) does the AI assistant use? How do you use them? Do you think they help improve your productivity?

Give 5 instances where AI model gave incorrect or misleading answers. You can use screenshots or copy-paste the Q&A.

I used Github Copilot on this assignment which runs on GPT-4.1 by default. I use the assistant by pressing tab when it suggests code, and then checking the suggested code for errors and fixing it. I think that AI assistants do help my productivity because it saves the time I would take to google syntax. Despite the improvement they may provide for productivity, it is important to pay close attention to the suggested code as AI assistants often make mistakes.

Here are 5 examples of Github Copilot giving incorrect or misleading answers:

Example 1: Question 3 Part 4: Copilot Suggestion:

for datafile in ~/mimic/hosp/{a,l,pa}*.gz do echo “$datafile: $(zcat < $datafile | wc -l) lines done

This line doesn’t close the double quote which will throw a syntax error.

Example 2: Question 3 Part 5: Github Copilot saw the part of the question prompt saying “Display the first few lines of admissions.csv.gz” and thought that this was asking for a text response instead of code so it autogenerated the following text:

“To display the first few lines of admissions.csv.gz, you can use the following command:”

Copilot failed to generate any code.

Example 3: Question 3 Part 8: Copilot Suggestion: gzip -dk < ~/mimic/hosp/labevents.csv.gz > ~/mimic/hosp/labevents.csv

Issue: This command writes the large uncompressed file directly into the MIMIC data directory. The assignment instructions discourage modifying or expanding the dataset folder and recommend creating temporary files in the working directory instead. Following the suggestion could clutter the data folder or risk accidental commits.

Correction: gzip -dk < ~/mimic/hosp/labevents.csv.gz > ./labevents.csv

Example 4: Question 5:

Bash code: echo {con,pre}{sent,fer}{s,ed}

Github Copilot’s Interpretation: The echo command with the brace expansion {con,pre}{sent,fer}{s,ed } produces the following output: consents consented confer confers confered confered.

Issue: The output that Copilot predicts is incorrect.

Example 5: Question 6:

Copilot suggested using an absolute file path.

Issue: Using an absolute path works only on my computer. When the homework is rendered on another machine (grader’s environment or GitHub), the image will not load because that file path does not exist there.

Correction: The image should be placed inside the homework repository and referenced with a relative path.
